description:
Sebuah laporan viral terkait hantavirus. Laporan itu mengatakan bahwa virus yang kini mewabah di kapal pesiar MV Hondius tersebut, merupakan efek samping dari vaksin Covid-19.

Mengutip Reuters Selasa (12/5/2026), ini terkait sebuah postingan luas tanggal 7 Mei di media sosial Facebook. Dibagikan tangkapan layar pengajuan Pfizer kepada Badan Pengawas Obat dan Makanan AS (FDA) pada tahun 2021 untuk mendapatkan lisensi biologis untuk vaksinnya.

"Daftar efek samping vaksin Covid Pfizer termasuk infeksi paru-paru hantavirus!" kata unggahan itu.

Narasi tersebut juga dibagikan di X. Disebutkan juga soal bagaimana vaksin Covid mengandung hantavirus.

"Referensi tentang infeksi paru-paru hantavirus dalam dokumen Pfizer terdapat pada halaman keempat dari lampiran sembilan halaman, yang berjudul 'Daftar Kejadian Buruk yang Menarik Perhatian Khusus'," tulis Reuters lagi memuat postingan viral tersebut yang merujuk vaksin Pfizer-BioNTech.

Meski demikian perusahaan membantah postingan ini. Isi surat bukan konfirmasi bahwa vaksin tersebut menyebabkan infeksi paru-paru hantavirus, kata juru bicara Pfizer, dalam sebuah email.

Sebenarnya, Inggris memberikan izin pemasaran penuh untuk vaksin Pfizer pada akhir tahun 2022 setelah meninjau keamanan, kemanjuran, dan informasi lainnya. Termasuk daftar kejadian buruk yang diidentifikasi memiliki hubungan sebab akibat dengan vaksin tersebut.

Kejadian buruk ini dipublikasikan, dalam tautan terbuka, yang dimuat pada brosur produk Pfizer. Hantavirus tidak disebutkan dalam tautan terbuka.

Intinya, tidak ada hantavirus dalam daftar bahan vaksin Covid Pfizer, yang sekarang disebut Comirnaty. Menurut situs web Pfizer, suntikan Comirnaty tidak mengandung virus hidup.

​ज़रा इसे गौर से सुनिए: 1996 में, जेफ किंडलर (Jeff Kindler) मैकडॉनल्ड्स के वाइस प्रेसिडेंट और सलाहकार थे, है ना? और फिर वो फाइज़र के CEO बन जाते हैं। मतलब... क्या सच में?!

​एक सेकंड के लिए इसे समझने की कोशिश करते हैं। वो पहले एक ऐसी कंपनी के लिए काम करते हैं जो मोटापा, मधुमेह (Diabetes) और दिल की बीमारियों जैसी कई स्वास्थ्य समस्याओं की वजह बनती है... और फिर वो उस कंपनी के CEO बन जाते हैं जो आपको उन्हीं बीमारियों का इलाज बेचती है?

​कोई ताज्जुब नहीं कि पश्चिम (West) इस्लाम से नफरत क्यों करता है। इस्लाम व्यापार में धोखेबाजी को पूरी तरह से वर्जित करता है। कुरान कहता है कि आपको ईमानदारी और निष्पक्षता के साथ व्यापार करना चाहिए। और इन सबसे ऊपर, इस्लाम शोषण और दूसरों को नुकसान पहुँचाकर मुनाफा कमाने की सख्त मनाही करता है।

Trading Direkt Healthcare tittar i det senaste avsnittet av programmet på rapporterna från bland annat Novo Nordisk, Pfizer och Attendo.

Novo Nordisk redovisade ett justerat rörelseresultat på 32,9 miljarder danska kronor i det första kvartalet. Utfallet var därmed 14% över ett konsensus som bolaget själva har samlat in. Samtidigt höjdes helårsprognosen för 2026.

Jefferies spår att Eli Lillys fetmaläkemedel Fundayo kommer att få ett lyft i försäljningssiffrorna i samband med att kommersiell tillgång via försäkringar väntas komma upp i mitten av maj.

Amerikanska Pfizer redovisade ett justerat resultat per aktie om 0:75 dollar i det första kvartalet. Analytikernas förväntningar var ett resultat på 0:72 dollar per aktie, enligt en snittprognos från S&P Global Market Intelligence.

Omsorgsbolaget Attendo redovisade ett ebita-resultat på 470 miljoner kronor i kvartalet. Utfallet var 8 procent bättre än snittförväntningarna av fem estimat gjord av Infront. Bolagets vd Martin Tivéus uppgav i rapporten att han ser resultat från bolagets förbättringsarbete.

Omsorgsbolaget Ambea har också rapporterat i veckan som gick. Rörelseresultatet var upp till 380 miljoner kronor från 277 miljoner kronor för samma kvartal för ett år sedan. DNB Carnegies analytiker påpekade i en fråga till Ambeas ledning att koncernens tidigare kommentarer kring ebita-marginalen verkar försiktiga med tanke på en stark start på 2026.

C-Rad, en underleverantör till strålterapisektorn, ökade orderingången med 19 procent i det första kvartalet till 115 miljoner kronor. Tillväxten drevs av regionerna Americas och Emea medan orderingången i Apac fortsatte vara svag.

Gubra har sänkt sina tillväxt- och marginalprognoser för sin så kallade CRO-verksamhet, som hjälper läkemedels- och bioteknikbranschen att genomföra prekliniska forskningsaktiviteter, för helåret 2026.

Danska Zealand Pharma redovisade ett rörelseresultat på -573 miljoner danska kronor. Helårsprognosen upprepades. I samband med rapporten kom bolaget med besked om ett återköpsprogram om 0,2 miljarder dollar motsvarande 1,3 miljarder danska kronor.

Trading Direkt Healthcare sänds varje måndag klockan 12.00 med fokus på de senaste händelserna inom life science.

title: 🐶 Zoetis: Defensive Tieraktie oder doch unter Druck?
description:
Zoetis ist der weltgrößte Anbieter von Tiergesundheitsprodukten und wurde 2013 von Pfizer abgespalten. Das Unternehmen verdient sein Geld vor allem mit verschreibungspflichtigen Medikamenten, Impfstoffen und Diagnostik für Haustiere und Nutztiere. Im ersten Quartal 2026 lag der Umsatz bei rund 2,3 Milliarden US-Dollar, ein Plus von 3 Prozent gegenüber dem Vorjahr. Gleichzeitig zeigte sich aber auch, dass das Geschäft aktuell nicht ganz so krisenfest wirkt, wie viele Anleger es lange angenommen hatten.

Denn genau bei der klassischen Investment-These für Zoetis gibt es gerade Risse: Reuters berichtet, dass preisbewusste Haustierbesitzer Tierarztbesuche verschieben und bei Premium-Behandlungen vorsichtiger werden. Damit bleibt Zoetis zwar ein spannender Qualitätswert im Bereich Tierpharma, aber der Markt schaut inzwischen deutlich kritischer darauf, wie robust dieses Geschäft wirklich durch ein schwierigeres Umfeld kommt.

title: Maintaining a State of Control in Biopharma: How EM and DES Work Together
description:
Environmental Monitoring (EM) and Disinfectant Efficacy Studies (DES) work together to maintain a state of control in biopharma manufacturing. EM provides continuous microbial and particulate data to identify trends, excursions, and potential root causes. DES validates the effectiveness of disinfectants against local organisms, surfaces, and contact times, supporting robust cleaning programs.

When used together, EM informs DES challenges and DES strengthens cleaning processes that EM later verifies. This integrated approach helps detect issues early, support regulatory compliance, improve cleaning strategies, and ensure aseptic environments remain safe and controlled for high‑quality product manufacturing.

title: [EN] - How to fix Europe's access gap in Biopharma
description:
Europe does not lack talent. It does not lack scientists. What it often lacks is structure.

Welcome to Pharma Minds, Mini-Series « Who controls innovation ? ». In this series, we explore one question in two parts: who controls innovation - and who actually makes it happen.

There is an alarming gap in global healthcare: more than 100 new drugs currently available in the United States are still not accessible to European patients. Why?  Because while Europe produces exceptional research, its access pathways are fragmented, and increasingly influenced by global pricing debates such as Most Favored Nation (MFN) policies.

In this episode, we tackle the execution gap with Pierre-Henri Belin, Co-Founder and CEO of Xcube.Bio. His company accelerates biopharma market entry across Europe by mitigating risks and bridging the gap between capital, deep expertise, and industry knowledge. 
Pierre-Henri shares a bold vision to pool resources, make Europe attractive for research again, and ensure that innovation actually reaches the people who need it.

Because research without access is only half a success.

In this episode, we cover:
◾️ The 100-Drug Gap: The alarming disparity between US and European patient access to new treatments.
◾️ The Root Causes: How fragmented regulatory systems and national-level decision-making are holding Europe back.
◾️ The Consequences: What this delay means for patients and the global competitiveness of Europe’s healthcare ecosystem.
◾️ The Solution: Pierre-Henri’s proposed model built on transparency, early collaboration, and shared responsibility.
◾️ A Path Forward: How Europe can reinvent its system and become a more predictable market without sacrificing safety or trust.

If Europe wants to remain a scientific leader, it must restructure. 
But this raises a deeper question: is the pharmaceutical economic model still aligned with the expectations of public health systems?

In this week's Stansberry Investor Hour, Dan and John Engel welcome Dave Lashmet to the show. Dave is the editor of Stansberry Venture Technology, an advisory that takes a "venture capitalist" look at the market. Dave scours the market looking for little-known small-cap companies that are potentially producing the next wonder drug or technology.

Dave kicks things off by discussing the first of three biopharmaceutical companies he's sharing that have monopolies in weight-loss drugs. He starts by showing how drugs gain their monopolies via patents, giving them "economic exclusivity." While companies might be targeting the same patients, the patents influence how they're being treated. The first company gains an edge by not only targeting folks suffering from obesity, but also by treating those with Type 2 diabetes. Dave also explains the contrast in mentality between the U.S. and other countries regarding obesity being preventable. And he provides info showing how obesity is a "slippery slope" and shares that a study found that participants who got off the drug gained back the weight they lost before.

Next, Dave sums up how the first company has cleared all of the risks and expenses from clinical trials, while a close competitor still has to get past its trials due to unknown side effects. When asked about why folks would stay on a weight-loss pill for life, Dave points to how our culture has drastically changed over the years, from actively working on farms to passively working in cubicles. These drugs help balance out the resulting shift. Dave then transitions into the next company that has a drug that focuses on fatty liver disease. He explains how this distinction helps the company gain its monopoly due to how irreplaceable livers are. And similar to the first company, this drug will have lifelong consumers. And the good news for investors is that its only competitor causes weight gain.

Finally, Dave presents the final company that tackles weight loss by focusing on genetics. Unlike the first two companies, this one treats patients with an injectable drug rather than a pill. However, it zeroes in on our natural "hunger switch," suppressing the users' appetites. Right now, the company is only waiting to get past trials, which puts it at a disadvantage compared with the other two. But Dave still believes that because of how it works, it's still set to stand beside the two pills.

description:
The DNA Data Revolution

The world is running out of space to store data. But the solution isn’t a bigger hard drive. It is inside you.

Right now, the world’s digital data—every movie, photo, and tweet ever created—would require a warehouse the size of several football fields to store.

Yet, you could fit all of that information into a single teaspoon of DNA.

DNA is nature’s ultimate hard drive. It is millions of times denser than any silicon chip.

While a hard drive might last ten years, DNA can preserve information for thousands of years without losing a single bit.

And here is the real twist.

Scientists have already successfully encoded entire books, music videos, and even computer viruses into synthetic DNA.

The next cloud storage provider won't be a massive data center. It might be a biological lab.

The future of technology is not just digital.

It is organic.

title: No More Blood Shortages? The Rise of Lab-Grown Oxygen Carriers
description:
In 2026, lab-grown synthetic oxygen carriers—engineered from recombinant hemoglobin and nano-encapsulated lipid systems—are being used in emergency trauma care to deliver oxygen when donated blood is unavailable. These universal, shelf-stable fluids require no refrigeration, work across all blood types, and carry zero risk of disease transmission. Deployed during the 2025 California wildfires and by U.S. military medics, they’ve stabilized critical patients until whole blood transfusions became possible.
⚠️ Critical Reality Check: These products are not full blood replacements. They do not clot, fight infection, or carry immune cells. Regulatory approvals (e.g., FDA “compassionate use,” EU CE Mark) limit them to acute trauma and emergency settings only. Human blood donation remains essential for surgeries, cancer care, and chronic conditions. Synthetic carriers address short-term oxygen delivery—not systemic blood needs.
🔔 Subscribe to Tomorrow Intelligence for scientifically precise, medically grounded coverage of biotech innovation, transfusion science, and breakthroughs that expand access without replacing humanity.
👍 Like, share, and hit the bell for weekly videos that reveal how intelligence, when merged with biology, can turn crisis into hope.

⚠️ COMPREHENSIVE DISCLAIMERS
Channel Disclaimer:
Tomorrow Intelligence is an independent educational channel. We are not affiliated with HbO2 Therapeutics, Sanguine Corp, the American Red Cross, or any biotech firm mentioned. Our content is based on peer-reviewed studies (The Lancet Haematology, 2025), FDA emergency use authorizations, and clinical trial data as of May 2026—not promotional material.
“Ending Human Donation Shortages” Clarification:
Synthetic oxygen carriers do not eliminate the need for human blood donation. They address acute oxygen transport only in emergencies. Over 90% of transfusion needs (e.g., platelets for leukemia, plasma for burns, red cells for surgery) still require human donors. The phrase refers to temporary gap-filling, not systemic replacement.
Technology Scope Disclaimer:
Current products (e.g., Hemospan derivatives, PEGylated hemoglobin) are acellular oxygen therapeutics, not artificial red blood cells. They lack nuclei, membranes, and biological functions beyond O₂/CO₂ exchange. No lab has yet created a fully functional synthetic erythrocyte.
Regulatory Status Disclaimer:
As of May 2026:
The U.S. FDA has not approved any synthetic blood product for routine use—only for compassionate/emergency protocols.
The EU grants CE Mark under Class III medical device rules for limited trauma indications.
No product is approved for civilian hospital stockpiling outside trials.
Military vs. Civilian Use:
The U.S. Department of Defense has procured units for battlefield use under IND (Investigational New Drug) exemptions—but this does not constitute broad approval. Civilian access remains restricted.
Safety & Side Effects Disclaimer:
Early-generation hemoglobin-based oxygen carriers (HBOCs) were linked to increased hypertension and oxidative stress. Newer nano-encapsulated versions show improved safety, but long-term effects are still under study. They are not risk-free.
Shelf Life & Logistics Claims:
While synthetic carriers are room-temperature stable for 1–2 years (vs. 42 days for RBCs), they are not infinitely durable. Degradation, aggregation, and oxidation remain challenges.

✔️ Control bleeding

title: Trump says he supports vaccines but raises concerns about how many are given
description:
Trump on vaccines and vaccine safety
ATTKISSON: Do you think there should be a vaccine safety commission?

TRUMP: A commission on what?

ATTKISSON: Vaccine safety, something to examine. Something like he proposed back then.

TRUMP: No. Look, I believe in vaccines, but I don't believe that you know, you have to have a mandate for all of them. The polio vaccine's amazing. It's, you know, wiped it out. And I believe in vaccines, but you know, I think we're up to 88 vaccines. And I really feel that if vaccines, they were given in smaller quantities. They want to cut some out and that's good too and I agree with that. 82 is too many. If you look at Denmark and other countries, you have 12, 14, I think 17. And we have like 82. But I look at these beautiful little babies and they get a vat, I mean, like a big glass of, of stuff pumped into their bodies. And I think it's a very negative thing to do.

title: AI Found a Drug in 30 Days That Scientists Couldn't in 12 Years
description:
For decades, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis has been a death sentence. A slow, suffocating lung disease with no cure, no clear cause, and a brutal track record of defeating every drug scientists threw at it. Researchers spent 12 years and billions of dollars trying to crack it. Billions. And they kept hitting walls.

Then an AI called Chemistry42 showed up and found a promising drug candidate in 30 days.

Not 30 months. Not 30 years. Thirty days.

And here's the part that should make your jaw drop — that molecule didn't just look good on paper. It actually made it to Phase II clinical trials, meaning real human beings responded well enough to it that scientists said "keep going." That almost never happens. The drug discovery process is a graveyard of promising ideas that collapse long before they ever reach a human body.

This changes everything about how we think about medicine.

Big pharma companies are now in a full sprint to build their own AI systems because the competitive math is simple and terrifying — if your rival can find a drug candidate in 30 days and you're still running traditional lab cycles, you're already behind. Not slightly behind. Catastrophically behind.

In this video, we break down exactly how Chemistry42 works, why AI is so uniquely powerful at finding molecules that human chemists would never think to try, and what this Phase II result actually means for the future of drug development.

And then we ask the question everyone in the scientific community is quietly debating right now — which disease should AI go after next?

Alzheimer's? Cancer? ALS? Something we haven't even named yet?

The race is on. And it's moving faster than most people realize.

title: PSIs Closed Loop Anti Aging Drug Discovery Engine
description:
Perplexity: "A Pharmaceutical Superintelligence (PSI) system could use multi-omic aging markers as an objective reward signal in a closed-loop “design → simulate → critique → redesign” process for anti-aging drugs.

Core idea
PSI would treat changes in epigenetics, microRNAs, and inflammatory markers as hard biological criteria for its CRITIC verify‑then‑correct loop. Using in silico twins and models like ClinicalGAN, it would simulate how each candidate molecule perturbs the epigenome and transcriptome, then reward or penalize chemical scaffolds accordingly.

Key feedback signals:
Senolytic microRNAs and p53 wiring
The system tracks whether a drug upregulates protective miRNAs like miR‑106b‑5p, which promotes p53 acetylation at K120, pushes p53 signaling toward pro‑apoptotic senolysis (via PUMA), and suppresses PCAF‑driven senescence. Candidates that reproduce this “youthful” miR‑106b‑5p/p53/PCAF profile get strong positive reward.

DNA methylation at multi‑omic aging genes:
PSI monitors age‑linked DNA methylation changes, especially at “multi‑omic aging genes” whose hypermethylation directly suppresses beneficial gene expression (e.g., CD248). The loop penalizes molecules that allow PRC2‑mediated promoter methylation to persist and rewards those that preserve youthful methylation patterns and DNAmAge signatures across tissues.

Restoration of epigenetic stability and heterochromatin:
Since aging erodes marks like H3K9me3 and de‑represses endogenous retroviruses (ERVs), the simulators check whether a candidate restores heterochromatin integrity, reduces ERV expression, and prevents genomic instability—analogous to or better than baseline metformin.

Suppression of inflammaging and epigenetic age acceleration:
The system evaluates impact on interferon signaling and inflammatory cytokines (CXCL9, CXCL10, CCL11, IL‑18) that causally drive epigenetic age acceleration and multimorbidity. Drugs that lower these markers and slow clocks such as GrimAge and PhenoAge are tagged as systemically anti‑aging.

The autonomous loop:
As generative models produce thousands of molecules, PSI runs kinetic and clinical simulations to generate multi‑omic readouts per candidate. CRITIC then asks, in effect: Does this compound upregulate miR‑106b‑5p, prevent CD248 methylation, restore H3K9me3, and lower CXCL9?

If no, the framework forces structural edits and re‑simulation.

If yes, it rewards that scaffold and uses it as a starting point for even stronger derivatives.

The result is a continuous, objective, multi‑omic optimization loop that aims to produce drugs that regress multiple aging clocks more powerfully and specifically than broad, low‑signal interventions like metformin."

title: AI Medicine’s Crystal Ball Problem: What GaiaLab’s Report Reveals
description:
AI in medicine is often described like a crystal ball — a system that can predict the next breakthrough drug, clinical trial, or therapeutic opportunity before the world catches up.

But GaiaLab’s Drug–Trial Concordance Report reveals a harder truth:

Not every AI “prediction” is actually a prediction.

In this video, we break down GaiaLab’s May 12, 2026 Drug–Trial Concordance Report, which evaluated 310 drug–trial matches across oncology and disease contexts.

The key finding:

Total matches: 310
Prospective predictions: 0
Retrospective matches: 310
Flagged signals: 88
Advisory notes: 19

That zero matters.

It shows why timestamp discipline is essential in AI medicine. If a clinical trial was already registered before an AI system logged the match, the result may still be useful — but it is retrospective concordance, not forward prediction.

In this episode, we explore:

Why AI medicine has a hindsight problem
Why concordance scores are not efficacy scores
Why a 64/100 score is not a 64% chance of success
Why flagged clinical-trial signals require careful interpretation
Why molecular panels are analytical context, not always enrollment criteria
Why trustworthy AI in drug discovery must separate signal, evidence, and proof

GaiaLab is building toward a more evidence-driven future for biomedical AI — one where predictions are measured by when they were logged, what was already public, and whether the system saw the signal before history made it obvious.

title: Changing paradigms in natural product discovery - with Paul Jensen.
description:
Cultured microbes are a traditional source of natural product-based medicines. Yet the vast majority of microbial diversity has yet to be cultured. This presentation will explore a new, culture independent approach to access "dark chemical space" and its potential as a source of new chemical diversity and drug leads.
Bio: Paul Jensen is a Professor at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography, Center for Marine Biotechnology and Biomedicine, University of California San Diego. His research interests lie at the interface of marine microbiology and natural products chemistry. His lab studies what marine microbes produce natural products, where they live, why they make them, and how to better exploit them for useful purposes including drug discovery. While working with cultured microorganisms is an important aspect of this research, “omic” approaches are providing important new insight into the extent of microbial diversity in marine habitats, how effectively it has been accessed for natural product discovery, and how environmental metabolomes shape community structure. His recent work includes new approaches to characterize unexplored marine chemical space while his interests in chemical ecology have helped shape our understating of the roles of natural products in predation defense. Paul holds a Ph.D. degree from the Scripps Institution of Oceanography, an M.S. degree from San Diego State University, and a B.S. degree from the Florida Institute of Technology.

title: THE POWER OF RINGS: Why Cyclic Peptides are the Future of Drug Discovery
description:
The pharmaceutical landscape is shifting. While linear peptides like GLP-1 agonists have seen explosive growth, cyclic peptides are the next frontier. By covalently closing the amino acid chain into a ring, these molecules gain incredible stability and binding affinity.
​Key Trends from CAS Data:
​Market Growth: The cyclic peptide market is projected to reach $5.3 billion by 2032, driven by oncology, autoimmune, and infectious disease research.
​The Oral Revolution: Historically, peptides had to be injected. Now, through N-methylation and advanced delivery devices like the "RaniPill," we are achieving clinically meaningful oral bioavailability.
​AI-Driven Design: New generative AI models and tools like AlphaFold3 are shortening discovery timelines from years to months by predicting the perfect ring architecture.
​Undruggable Targets: Cyclic peptides are uniquely suited to disrupt protein-protein interactions (PPIs) that traditional small molecules simply cannot reach.
​From macrocycles to bicyclic structures, the versatility of these molecular rings is unlocking new treatments for cancer, metabolic disorders, and rare diseases.

description:
Send us Fan Mail (https://www.buzzsprout.com/1906263/fan_mail/new) 


The clinical trial system is starting to look like a motorway at a standstill: more and more drugs are lining up, but the lanes ahead are already full. We sit down with Pamela Tenart to unpack why the industry may have reached the limit of human-only clinical development, and why “adding more people” is no longer a realistic plan when experienced CRAs, site co-ordinators and trial operators are already stretched thin.

From there, we get practical about what agentic AI could change inside clinical trial operations. We talk about AI agents that can pull context across CTMS, EDC, safety reporting and TMF, helping monitors prepare for site visits, flag missing fields, propose next best actions, draft communications, and reduce the dead time where teams are simply waiting for updates. The point is not to automate judgement, but to automate the admin and co-ordination work so humans can focus on strategy, enrolment, quality, and patient safety with a clear audit trail and human-in-the-loop control.

We also zoom out to the bigger bottleneck: sponsors, CROs and sites are part of one connected system, so optimising one party can just shift the pain elsewhere. Along the way we explore why better, more sensitive endpoints can shorten trial timelines, how policy and regulation might need to evolve, and a memorable metaphor from industrial history: electricity boosted individual productivity first, but factories only truly improved once they were rebuilt for the new technology.

If you’re working in clinical research, drug development, biotech, or health tech, this conversation will help you think more clearly about where AI genuinely shortens the critical path and where it simply adds noise. title: The reality of data fragmentation in clinical trials with Kavita Gaadhe
description:
In this episode of Clinical Data Talks, Sylvain Berthelot welcomes Dr. Kavita Gaadhe, a clinical data management lead working at the high-stakes intersection of technology and precision medicine. Together, they explore the increasingly complex reality of managing non-linear data flows in a digitalized landscape.

She explains the friction that occurs when these heterogeneous sources "speak different languages," forcing data teams to spend their days reconciling time points and bridging semantic gaps to meet standardization requirements.


Sylvain and Kavita discuss why the industry is currently attempting to bolt 21st-century data onto 20th-century infrastructure, the necessity of viewing data as a strategic asset rather than a byproduct, and why oncology and precision medicine trials demand flexibility from technology first and foremost.

title: Electrifying the Factory: Agentic AI For Faster Clinical Trials with Pamela Tenaerts
description:
The clinical trial system is starting to look like a motorway at a standstill: more and more drugs are lining up, but the lanes ahead are already full. We sit down with Pamela Tenart to unpack why the industry may have reached the limit of human-only clinical development, and why “adding more people” is no longer a realistic plan when experienced CRAs, site co-ordinators and trial operators are already stretched thin.

From there, we get practical about what agentic AI could change inside clinical trial operations. We talk about AI agents that can pull context across CTMS, EDC, safety reporting and TMF, helping monitors prepare for site visits, flag missing fields, propose next best actions, draft communications, and reduce the dead time where teams are simply waiting for updates. The point is not to automate judgement, but to automate the admin and co-ordination work so humans can focus on strategy, enrolment, quality, and patient safety with a clear audit trail and human-in-the-loop control.

We also zoom out to the bigger bottleneck: sponsors, CROs and sites are part of one connected system, so optimising one party can just shift the pain elsewhere. Along the way we explore why better, more sensitive endpoints can shorten trial timelines, how policy and regulation might need to evolve, and a memorable metaphor from industrial history: electricity boosted individual productivity first, but factories only truly improved once they were rebuilt for the new technology.

If you’re working in clinical research, drug development, biotech, or health tech, this conversation will help you think more clearly about where AI genuinely shortens the critical path and where it simply adds noise. title: Glow Blend (BPC-157 + TB4 + GHK-Cu): Three Peptides, Zero Combined Clinical Research #shorts
description:
The Glow Blend is a three-peptide combination product widely sold in the wellness and skincare gray market, combining BPC-157, TB4 (typically the TB-500 fragment), and GHK-Cu. The individual peptide components have meaningfully different evidence bases. The combined three-peptide blend has no published clinical trial data. Here's the documented research for each component, and what the combined evidence does and doesn't show.

Components covered:
- BPC-157: synthetic 15-amino-acid pentadecapeptide, fragment of a larger Body Protection Compound protein found in human gastric juice. Over 80% of published research from the Sikiric laboratory at the University of Zagreb. Mostly animal model evidence. Currently on the FDA July 23, 2026 PCAC agenda for review of inclusion on the 503A bulks list.

- TB4 / TB-500: TB4 in research peptide labeling almost always refers to the TB-500 fragment (LKKTETQ), a synthetic 7-amino-acid peptide derived from thymosin beta-4. This is NOT the full-length thymosin beta-4 protein (43 amino acids), which RegeneRx Biopharmaceuticals advanced through Phase 2 trials for cardiac and dry eye indications. The TB-500 fragment sold by research peptide vendors has substantially different clinical evidence than the full-length thymosin beta-4 used in registered trials. Currently on the FDA July 23, 2026 PCAC agenda.

- GHK-Cu: copper-binding tripeptide (glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine plus copper-2 ion). Discovered by Dr. Loren Pickart at UCSF in 1973. Naturally present in human blood plasma at approximately 200 ng/mL at age 20, declining to 80 ng/mL by age 60. Over 50 years of published research. The substantial human clinical evidence base derives primarily from topical formulations — multiple randomized controlled trials at 1-2% topical concentrations. To my knowledge, no published randomized controlled trials test injectable GHK-Cu for any indication in humans. Injectable GHK-Cu is on the FDA February 2027 PCAC agenda.

In this Short:
- What's actually in the Glow Blend vial (BPC-157, TB4 fragment, GHK-Cu at 10mg total)
- Why "TB4" in research peptide labels typically refers to the TB-500 fragment, not full thymosin beta-4
- The substantial difference between the TB-500 fragment and the full-length thymosin beta-4 used in RegeneRx Phase 2 trials
- The single-laboratory concentration of BPC-157 research (over 80% from Sikiric et al., University of Zagreb)
- The topical vs injectable evidence gap for GHK-Cu (50 years of topical research, almost no injectable RCTs)
- The theoretical rationale for combining the three peptides (different repair/recovery/regeneration pathways)
- Why no published randomized controlled trials have studied this specific three-peptide combination in humans
- The parallel to the Beauty Blend (GHK-Cu + KPV) evidence gap
- The parallel to the BPC-157 + TB-500 blend evidence gap
- The regulatory status: BPC-157 and TB-500 on FDA July 2026 PCAC agenda, injectable GHK-Cu on FDA February 2027 PCAC agenda

Research referenced:
- BPC-157: Sikiric P et al. - foundational pentadecapeptide research (1990s-present, University of Zagreb)
- BPC-157: PMC11859134 - 2025 comprehensive review noting "no sequence homology with known intestinal peptides"
- TB-500: Smart M et al. - LKKTETQ fragment characterization vs full thymosin beta-4
- Thymosin beta-4: RegeneRx Phase 2 trials (cardiac, dry eye disease, pressure ulcers)
- GHK-Cu: Pickart L. - 1973 discovery thesis (UCSF)
- GHK-Cu: Pickart L et al. - "Regenerative and Protective Actions of the GHK-Cu Peptide in the Light of the New Gene Data" - Int J Mol Sci, 2018 (PMC6073405)
- GHK-Cu: Multiple topical clinical trials (Leyden et al., Abdulghani et al., Finkley et al.)

- The PB Pick designation is a vendor-level recommendation, not a peptide-level recommendation
- For viewers researching this category despite the combined evidence gap, EZ Peptides is the disclosed vendor: ezpeptides.com with code BENCHMARK for 10% off

title: Tamiflu: $1.5B in pills. Half the evidence was hidden. #Shorts
description:
Governments worldwide stockpiled oseltamivir (Tamiflu) for pandemic preparedness based on Kaiser et al. 2003 (Arch Intern Med), which pooled industry-supplied trial summaries and reported a halving of hospitalisations and complications. Stockpile cost: ~£473 million in the UK alone; ~$1.5 billion globally.

In 2009, the BMJ + Cochrane (Tom Jefferson, Peter Doshi, Mark Jones) asked Roche for the underlying clinical study reports (CSRs). Roche refused for nearly four years. After sustained public pressure and BMJ campaigning, the CSRs were released in 2013.

The Cochrane 2014 re-analysis (Jefferson T et al. BMJ 2014;348:g2545; Cochrane CD008965) from the full CSRs:
• Complication reduction (hospitalisations etc.): RR ~0.95 [0.78, 1.16] — not significantly different from placebo
• Symptom-duration: ~16 hours shorter (statistically significant; clinically marginal)
• Adverse events: psychiatric, renal, GI signals previously underreported

The meta-analysis lesson: OUTCOME-REPORTING BIAS — within-trial selective publication — is invisible to funnel plots and Egger tests (which only detect missing TRIALS, not missing OUTCOMES). The fix is access to clinical study reports plus tools like Cochrane's RoB-ME (risk of bias due to missing evidence, Page 2023). EMA, FDA, and Health Canada now require CSR access for HTA. The All Trials campaign and the Restoring Invisible and Abandoned Trials (RIAT) initiative grew directly from this case.

Sources:
• Kaiser L et al. Arch Intern Med 2003;163:1667-72 (industry-summary MA)
• Jefferson T et al. BMJ 2014;348:g2545 (full-CSR Cochrane re-analysis)
• Doshi P, Jefferson T, Del Mar C. PLOS Med 2012;9:e1001201 (data access campaign)
• Page MJ et al. RoB-ME, BMJ 2023 (risk of bias due to missing evidence)

Methodological note: Kaiser 2003 pooled point estimate and Cochrane 2014 CSR pool are illustrative; the qualitative reversal is the substantive finding documented in the Cochrane review and BMJ campaign.

title: Time Machine Models in Platform Trials | Berry Consultants
description:
Platform trials face the same challenge as comparing Jack Nicklaus to Scottie Scheffler. But as Dr. Scott Berry explains, this gap in eras can be bridged.

When treatments enter a platform trial at different times, we can't just compare raw data from early arms to late arms. The solution is to use time machine models. title: CAST 1989: drugs that suppressed PVCs tripled mortality. #Shorts
description:
The Cardiac Arrhythmia Suppression Trial (CAST), published in NEJM in 1991, is the foundational case study in the surrogate-endpoint trap.

The surrogate (PVC suppression at 24 hours): encainide and flecainide reduced ventricular ectopy by 70-75%. RR ~0.27 [0.20, 0.35].

The real outcome (all-cause mortality, CAST-I + CAST-II): same drugs INCREASED death by ~3-fold. RR ~3.0 [1.8, 5.0]. Trial halted early. Estimated 50,000+ excess deaths in the years before CAST was run.

The meta-analysis lesson: a surrogate endpoint is a causal HYPOTHESIS about a biomarker. It is NOT the patient outcome. When meta-analyses pool surrogate endpoints (PVC suppression, LDL-C reduction, HbA1c lowering, BP reduction, viral load), the pooled effect tells you what the drug did to the surrogate — never what it did to the patient.

Real-world echoes of CAST:
• Niacin → lowered LDL but no CV benefit (AIM-HIGH, HPS2-THRIVE)
• Torcetrapib → raised HDL but increased mortality
• Rosiglitazone → improved HbA1c but increased MI
• Bezafibrate / fenofibrate → mixed surrogate-to-outcome translation

The Cochrane Handbook §1.3 lists CAST as the canonical example of why meta-analyses on hard outcomes outrank meta-analyses on surrogates.

Sources:
• Echt DS et al. NEJM 1991;324:781-8 (CAST-I, RR 3.6 [1.7, 8.5] for death)
• CAST-II Investigators. NEJM 1992;327:227-33 (moricizine, RR 2.5)
• Fleming TR, DeMets DL. Ann Intern Med 1996;125:605-13 ("Surrogate end points in clinical trials: are we being misled?")
• Bucher HC et al. JAMA 1999;282:771-8 (surrogate-vs-outcome MA methodology)

Methodological note: individual point estimates illustrative; CAST-I exact published RR is in source.

title: Frozen Shoulder: What the World’s Largest Clinical Trial Reveals About Surgery vs. Therapy
description:
PHYSIO MOSMAN: https://www.fitasaphysio.com/

The UK FROST study was a multicentre randomised clinical trial conducted to determine the most effective treatment for adults suffering from primary frozen shoulder. Researchers compared three common interventions: early structured physiotherapy with a steroid injection, manipulation under anaesthesia, and arthroscopic capsular release. The trial findings revealed that none of the treatments were clinically superior to the others regarding long-term pain relief and improved shoulder function at the one-year mark. While capsular release surgery carried the highest risks and costs, manipulation under anaesthesia was identified as the most cost-effective option within the UK healthcare system. The rise of radiopharmaceuticals represents one of the most exciting frontiers in oncology, yet it introduces a level of logistical complexity that traditional Clinical Supply Chain and RTSM systems were never designed to handle. Because these materials decay in hours rather than months, the operational window for patient administration is incredibly narrow, leaving zero margin for error. Success in these trials depends entirely on the seamless orchestration of manufacturing, logistics and site readiness. 

This webinar explores the unique architecture required for a high-performing radiopharmaceutical RTSM. The featured speakers begin with a comprehensive overview of the radiopharmaceutical landscape, identifying the specific constraints, such as just-in-time manufacturing and rigorous cold-chain requirements, that differentiate these products from standard Investigational Medicinal Products (IMPs). 

A core focus of the session is Smart RTSM Design. In the high-stakes environment of nuclear medicine, there is a temptation to over-engineer systems. The session will discuss how to build what is functionally “needed” to ensure supply integrity, rather than a “wish list” of features that add unnecessary friction. By prioritizing lean, responsive system logic, study teams can ensure that the “Right Kit, Right Patient, Right Time” mantra becomes a reality even under extreme time pressure. 

Beyond the technical, the speakers will address the human element of clinical trials. Shifts in study personnel and leadership roles can create ripples of misalignment in long-term programs. They will also examine how a robust RTSM framework acts as a “source of truth,” providing continuity and operational stability even as internal teams evolve. 

Finally, the webinar will tackle the inevitability of change through Advanced Amendment Management. In the world of Radiopharma, protocol pivots and supply chain disruptions are not a matter of “if,” but “when.” The speakers will share strategies for building an RTSM that is inherently flexible, allowing for rapid configuration changes without compromising the study’s data integrity or timelines.

title: iMetaMed | Mapping HFpEF Pharmacotherapies Global Landscape: ClinicalTrials.gov Analysis 2003-2025
description:
DOI:
https://doi.org/10.1002/imm3.70042

RESEARCH ARTICLE
Open Access
Mapping the Global Clinical Landscape of Pharmacological Therapies for Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction: An Analysis Based on ClinicalTrials.gov (2003–2025)
Yucheng Hou, Jingwei Zhao, Yuqian Tang, Tan Liu, Zhiao Zhang, Ziheng Wang, Han Shen

ABSTRACT
Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) accounts for approximately 50% of global heart failure cases yet lacks robust pharmacological options. This analysis maps HFpEF drug trials registered on ClinicalTrials.gov from 2003 to 2025. A systematic search conducted on November 10, 2025, identified HFpEF-specific drug trials (LVEF ≥ 50%). Data regarding geography, phases, status, time, and drug classes were descriptively analyzed using R (version 4.3.1). Of the 272 trials, 236 qualified, with a notable surge post-2016 (180 [76.3%]). The majority were U.S.-led (138 [58.5%]). Phase Ⅱ trials were predominant, comprising 92 trials (39.0%), with 111 trials completed (47.0%) and 36 trials terminated (15.2%). The leading classes of drugs included SGLT2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) and novel/targeted therapies, each represented in 31 trials (13.1%). The period from 2021 to 2025 highlighted a focus on SGLT2i (30 trials, or 27.8%) and an increase in GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RA), following recent approvals (sacubitril/valsartan in 2021; empagliflozin/dapagliflozin in 2022–2023; and finerenone by the FDA in 2025). The expansion of trials post-2016 favors metabolic and targeted agents. However, attrition rates underscore the need to prioritize phenotype-specific and combination trials.

Summary
A post-2016 surge in HFpEF trials is predominantly led by the United States.

Research focus has shifted towards metabolic drugs like SGLT2i and GLP-1RA.

Phenotype-targeted strategies are crucial to address heterogeneity and high trial attrition.

title: Sports and Clinical Trials: The 1927 Yankees, 15 Tarzans, and Modern Athletes
description:
In this episode of "In the Interim…", Dr. Scott Berry examines the analytical challenges of comparing performance across eras in both sports and clinical research. Drawing from statistically robust family debates and published research, Scott details how overlapping competitors—such as athletes who played with both Babe Ruth, played with the next generation, who played with …  all the way to playing with Aaron Judge—enable the estimation of temporal effects and allow for objective comparisons between generations. He translates this approach directly into platform clinical trials, demonstrating how overlapping trial arms or shared control groups make it possible to quantify and adjust for time trends. Scott distinguishes between observable, model-based comparisons and subjective judgments, rigorously addressing limitations such as interactions between treatments and era, and emphasizing the foundational importance of empirical overlap over speculative claims.

*Key Highlights*
+ Deconstruction of time-machine thought experiments: analyzing how teams like the 1927 Yankees or athletes such as Johnny Weissmuller and Jesse Owens compare to present-day counterparts using statistical benchmarks.
+ Technical explanation of connecting eras empirically through players or trial arms who span multiple time periods, thereby supporting quantitative estimation of temporal shifts.
+ Detailed account of linear and hierarchical modeling strategies, with covariate adjustment for player age, period effects, and evolving population composition across baseball, hockey, and golf data.
+ Translation of these statistical constructs to adaptive and platform clinical trials, exemplified by I-SPY 2, where overlapping treatment and control arms permit rigorous assessment of evolving treatment effects over a trial’s lifespan.
+ Critical discussion of the rare but important possibility of treatment-by-era interactions, and the necessity of data-driven assessment rather than assumption.
+ Consideration of how these methods inform not just debates about athletic greatness and Hall of Fame inclusion, but also robust interpretation of treatment effects in longitudinal clinical studies.

title: Bivamelagon and RM-718: Rhythm Pharma's Next-Gen MC4R Agonists After Imcivree #shorts
description:
Setmelanotide (Imcivree) is the FDA-approved MC4R agonist for genetic obesity disorders, currently priced at approximately $420,000 per year and requiring daily subcutaneous injections. Rhythm Pharmaceuticals is developing two next-generation MC4R agonists that could fundamentally change the patient experience: bivamelagon (oral) and RM-718 (weekly, MC1R-sparing). Both are currently in clinical development. Here's where each compound stands as of 2026.

Compounds covered:
- Bivamelagon (formerly LB54640): Oral MC4R agonist in-licensed by Rhythm from LG Chem (South Korea). Phase 2 trial in 28 patients with acquired hypothalamic obesity, completed July 2025. Statistically significant and clinically meaningful BMI reductions at 14 weeks across 200, 400, and 600 mg oral daily doses. Most common adverse events: mild diarrhea, nausea. Some mild hyperpigmentation observed (4 patients, including 1 on placebo). Rhythm is refining the formulation before Phase 3 initiation.

- RM-718: Investigational weekly MC4R-specific agonist developed internally at Rhythm. Designed to be highly selective for MC4R while sparing MC1R, which is the receptor responsible for setmelanotide's skin hyperpigmentation side effect. Phase 1 trial first patient dosed March 2024. December 2025: Phase 1 Part D arm initiated for Prader-Willi syndrome patients, 26-week open-label, up to 20 patients. ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT06239116.

In this Short:
- What MC4R is (melanocortin-4 receptor, G-protein-coupled receptor in hunger/energy regulation)
- Why MC4R pathway mutations cause hyperphagia and severe early-onset obesity
- Setmelanotide's pricing reality and patient experience limitations
- Bivamelagon's oral administration advantage
- Bivamelagon's Phase 2 results (July 2025, ENDO meeting late-breaking abstract)
- Why bivamelagon's BMI reductions were "consistent with setmelanotide in similar patient populations"
- Why bivamelagon's tolerability profile is consistent with MC4R agonism
- RM-718's MC1R-sparing engineering goal (no hyperpigmentation)
- RM-718's weekly dosing schedule
- RM-718's Phase 1 timeline (March 2024 first patient, December 2025 PWS arm)
- The Prader-Willi syndrome opportunity for both compounds
- The potential for setmelanotide pricing pressure as next-generation compounds advance
- Rhythm's broader pipeline approach (preclinical congenital hyperinsulinism program)

Bivamelagon Phase 2 trial design and results:
- Trial design: randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind
- Population: patients aged 12 years and older with acquired hypothalamic obesity (n=28)
- Acquired hypothalamic obesity: typically caused by brain tumors, traumatic brain injury, or other hypothalamic damage
- Doses: 200 mg, 400 mg, or 600 mg oral daily, or placebo
- Duration: 14 weeks (randomized portion)
- Primary endpoint: change from baseline in BMI at 14 weeks
- Result: Statistically significant and clinically meaningful BMI reductions across all three dose levels
- Magnitude: "consistent with BMI reductions achieved with setmelanotide therapy in similar patient populations"
- Adverse events: mostly mild or grade 1 diarrhea and nausea
- Discontinuations: one patient discontinued due to serious adverse event (rectal bleeding)
- Hyperpigmentation: mild localized hyperpigmentation in 4 patients, including 1 placebo
- Patients may continue treatment in 52-week open-label extension

RM-718 program details:
- Investigational New Drug (IND) submission: late 2023
- Phase 1 first patient dosed: March 2024
- Trial registration: NCT06239116
- Phase 1 Part D arm initiated: December 2025
- Population: patients with Prader-Willi syndrome (up to 20 patients)
- Duration: 26-week open-label
- Differentiation from setmelanotide: MC1R-sparing design (no hyperpigmentation)
- Differentiation from setmelanotide: weekly subcutaneous administration vs daily

Disclaimer: Bivamelagon (LB54640) and RM-718 are investigational pharmaceutical compounds in clinical development. Neither is FDA approved for any indication. Phase 2 (bivamelagon) and Phase 1 (RM-718) results are preliminary and do not guarantee Phase 3 success or regulatory approval. Setmelanotide (Imcivree) remains the only FDA-approved MC4R agonist as of 2026. Patient access to next-generation MC4R agonists will depend on successful late-stage clinical development and FDA review processes. Did you know the FDA just approved a new weight-loss pill... that helped people lose over 11% of their body weight in a major trial? It’s called orforglipron, and it works in the same drug family as the famous weekly injections. These medicines mimic GLP-1... a natural hormone that tells your brain you’re full sooner, helping reduce hunger without constant willpower. But here’s why this is DIFFERENT. Until now, the strongest GLP-1 treatments were mostly injections... or pills with strict rules that made them hard to use. Empty stomach. Almost no water. Then wait before eating. Orforglipron changes that. In a study of more than 3,000 adults, people on the highest dose lost an average of 11.2% of their body weight... about 25 pounds... over 16 months. That’s not quite the 21% seen with some injectables... But for a simple daily pill, it’s a MAJOR shift. And the real breakthrough may be convenience. Because this is a small-molecule drug, it can be taken morning or night... with food or without. And for many people, that flexibility could be what makes treatment sustainable. But it may go beyond weight. Researchers also saw improvements in blood pressure... and cholesterol. And because of that potential, the FDA fast-tracked approval in just 50 days. Of course, it isn’t magic. Side effects... and cost... still matter. But the era of weight-loss shots being the only serious option may be ending. And we may be entering a new chapter... where powerful appetite control comes in a pill that fits in your pocket.

title: The Word They Never Wrote in the Application | Back in the Day
description:
The FDA approved the pill in 1960. The application never used the word 'contraceptive.'

On May 9, 1960, the FDA approved Enovid as a period treatment — its developers called it a contraceptive.

'Contraceptive' never appeared in the application. It's now in 150 million medicine cabinets.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
📅 May 9, 1960
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

📖 Full story below. 👇

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

THE FULL STORY

The FDA approved the birth control pill in 1960 — after an application that never once used the word 'contraceptive.' More than 150 million women take it daily today. The story of how it got approved is the story of a government pretending not to know what it was approving.

In 1950s America, contraception was illegal in several states under Comstock laws. Discussing birth control in public was taboo — even among doctors. G.D. Searle's lawyers knew a straightforward contraceptive application would be rejected. So they filed it for something else entirely.

Researcher Gregory Pincus — who had been fired from Harvard in 1937 for his fertilization experiments — chose Puerto Rico for the trials. It was densely populated, poor, and had no laws against contraception. The women were told only that the pills prevented pregnancy, not that this was an experimental clinical trial.

On May 9, 1960, the FDA approved Enovid — officially for 'menstrual disorders and infertility,' not contraception. Commissioner George Larrick signed off on an application built on a legal fiction everyone in the room understood. The pill was approved. The word 'contraceptive' never appeared.

Within five years, 6.5 million American women were taking the pill. By the 1970s it had become the most studied drug in history. The women in Puerto Rico whose consent had never been sought heard about it the same way everyone else did — through the news.

The word they refused to write in 1960 is now used 150 million times a day. Pincus — the man Harvard fired for crossing a line in 1937 — crossed a far larger one in Puerto Rico two decades later and built the most consequential drug of the 20th century.

What is ZURZUVAE® (zuranolone) CIV?
ZURZUVAE is a prescription medicine used to treat adults with postpartum depression (PPD).
What is the most important information I should know about ZURZUVAE?
ZURZUVAE may cause serious side effects, including:
• Decreased awareness and alertness, which can affect your ability to drive safely or do other dangerous activities. Don’t drive or do other dangerous activities until at least 12 hours after taking each dose during your 14‑day treatment course. You may not be able to tell on your own if you can drive safely or how much ZURZUVAE is affecting you.
• Sleepiness, drowsiness, slow thinking, dizziness, confusion, and trouble walking which could increase your risk for falls during treatment. Taking alcohol, or medicines like opioids while taking ZURZUVAE can make these symptoms worse and may also cause trouble breathing.
• ZURZUVAE and other antidepressants may increase the risk of suicidal thoughts or actions in people 24 years of age and younger.
• ZURZUVAE is not for use in children.
The most common side effects of ZURZUVAE include:
• Sleepiness or drowsiness, dizziness, common cold, diarrhea, feeling tired, weak, or having no energy, and urinary tract infection

Postpartum depression (PPD) is one of the most common medical conditions associated with pregnancy — and it’s treatable.

If diagnosed with PPD, talk to a healthcare provider and ask about 14‑day ZURZUVAE.

description:
The FDA authorized the first fruit-flavored vapes for adults 21 and over amid President Donald Trump’s previous vows to “save” vaping.

The agency green-lit electronic cigarettes from Los Angeles-based Glas in mango, blueberry and two varieties of menthol. The news came hours after the Wall Street Journal reported that Trump pressed FDA Commissioner Marty Makary to approve flavored vapes.

The approval marks a shift after the FDA for years worked aggressively to regulate flavored vapes, rejecting more than 1 million fruit-, candy- and dessert-flavored products, according to court filings. Nicotine companies had sued the FDA saying it unfairly shifted its standards for authorizing electronic cigarette liquids popular with teens. The Supreme Court last April unanimously backed the agency. Caption from reporting by Rachel Roubein.

Doctors Just Stopped Parkinson’s Tremors Instantly Without Surgery 🧠

This breakthrough medical technology is leaving millions shocked online. Patients with severe Parkinson’s tremors are experiencing immediate relief in real time without open brain surgery or implants.

Using MR-guided focused ultrasound (MRgFUS), doctors target a tiny area deep inside the brain while monitoring everything live through MRI imaging. The result looks almost unreal: uncontrollable shaking suddenly becomes steady movement within moments.

This non-invasive treatment uses highly focused ultrasound waves to precisely treat the brain region responsible for tremors. Patients remain awake during the procedure and can instantly test their movement while doctors observe the changes live.

For many people living with tremor-dominant Parkinson’s disease, this technology could represent a major step forward in improving daily life and restoring independence.

Researchers continue studying the long-term effectiveness and safety of this treatment, but the real-time before-and-after results are already capturing worldwide attention.

title: India’s Cheap Drugs: The Real Reason Global Healthcare Scales
description:
In this episode of Medical Historian, we explore the hidden system behind modern medicine: the global drug supply chain. What looks like cheap medicine is actually a massive international network connecting factories, chemical production, shipping routes, and geopolitical power — with India at the center as the “pharmacy of the world.”

As pharmaceutical manufacturing shifted away from the United States and Europe, India became one of the largest suppliers of affordable generic medicine on Earth. But this transformation reshaped more than healthcare costs — it changed how nations manage dependence, resilience, and medical security.

From global outsourcing to the fragility exposed during the COVID-19 pandemic, this episode reveals the invisible infrastructure quietly keeping millions alive every day.

History has the answers — and I’ll show you where to look.

🔍 Key Facts & Insights
• India became one of the world’s largest exporters of affordable generic medicine, supplying healthcare systems across both developed and developing nations.
• A large portion of Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (APIs) used globally are manufactured in China before being processed into finished medicines elsewhere.
• The modern pharmaceutical system depends heavily on global shipping, industrial manufacturing, and uninterrupted trade routes.
• Generic drug production dramatically lowered healthcare costs and expanded access to medicine worldwide.
• Pharmaceutical manufacturing increasingly moved overseas during the late twentieth century as globalization accelerated.
• Drug shortages can emerge from factory shutdowns, shipping disruptions, geopolitical tensions, or supply-chain concentration.
• The COVID-19 pandemic exposed how vulnerable many countries had become to disruptions in medical supply networks.
• Governments increasingly view pharmaceutical manufacturing as strategic infrastructure tied to national resilience and security.

📚 Further Reading

• Bottle of Lies by Katherine Eban — an investigation into the global generic drug industry and pharmaceutical manufacturing practices.
• The Truth Pill by Dinesh S. Thakur and Prashant Reddy T. — explores regulation, generic medicine, and the globalization of pharmaceuticals.
• Empire of Pain by Patrick Radden Keefe — examines the business structures and incentives shaping modern pharmaceutical systems.
• The World for Sale by Javier Blas and Jack Farchy — explores the global commodity networks and trade systems underpinning modern economies.
If this gave you a new perspective, hit subscribe.
History has the answers — and I’ll show you where to look.

title: The Hidden Truth About Generic Drug Prices in America
description:
Generic drugs are supposed to be the cheapest part of the U.S. healthcare system—chemically identical to brand-name medications, available after patents expire, and driven by competition.

But in practice, that’s not always what happens.

Over the past decade, regulators, hospitals, and state attorneys general have uncovered repeated cases where the prices of certain generic drugs spiked dramatically—sometimes overnight—despite no change in formulation or demand.

This video breaks down:

How the generic drug system is supposed to work
Why real-world pricing doesn’t always follow competitive logic
The structural reasons certain drugs remain expensive
And how these patterns led to massive antitrust investigations and lawsuits across the U.S.

This is not about one company or one scandal—it’s about how pricing behaves in thin, highly regulated pharmaceutical markets where competition is limited and entry barriers are high.

What looks like “cheap medicine” on paper often operates under a far more complex economic and legal structure than most consumers realize.

title: 251: Why a Single Large DoE Fails Biosimilar Glycan Optimization — And the Parallel Screening Met...
description:
Are you stuck screening endless compounds in biosimilar development and still not hitting your quality targets? Efficient compound screening is one of the toughest bottlenecks in biopharma, with outdated methods slowing progress and risking critical quality attributes in monoclonal antibody development.


David Brühlmann breaks down a practical, parallel framework for rapid compound screening that addresses interaction effects, masking, and data quality. Methods proven in challenging biosimilar development programs.


Topics discussed:

  •  The historical bottleneck of one-at-a-time screening in drug discovery and the impact of high throughput methods (01:04)
  •  Problems with both one-factor-at-a-time and large design of experiments approaches when handling many variables (02:10)
  •  Description of the parallel group method: splitting 17 quality modulating compounds into five biologically relevant groups and running experiments in parallel (06:09)
  •  How grouping compounds by biological mechanism improves interpretability and experimental design (06:43)
  •  Strategies for minimizing dilution effects, toxicity risks, and masking in multi-factor screens (08:24)
  •  The importance of multivariate analysis: using principal component analysis (PCA), Mahalanobis distance, and decision trees to interpret and select optimal experimental conditions (10:31)
  •  Real-world outcomes: identifying optimal compound combinations in just two rounds of screening (15:20)
  •  Reflections on the evolving role of hybrid modeling and machine learning in biosimilar process optimization (15:54)

In Part 2, the focus shifts to a hands-on approach, covering how to design compound groups based on biology, set concentration ranges without compromising data quality, and execute a 96-well screen with the rigor the method demands. It also highlights three key aspects that would be approached differently if the study were conducted today.


Strategic insight:


Effective compound screening shifts from one-at-a-time testing to biology-driven parallel grouping combined with multivariate analytics, enabling faster identification of optimal combinations while preserving data quality and capturing interaction effects.


If you want more detail, you can read the full article “Parallel experimental design and multivariate analysis provides efficient screening of cell culture media supplements to improve biosimilar product quality (https://www.researchgate.net/publication/313729525_Parallel_experimental_design_and_multivariate_analysis_provides_efficient_screening_of_cell_culture_media_supplements_to_improve_Biosimilar_product_quality) ” published in Biotechnology and Bioengineering, which outlines the methods and findings behind this approach.

title: Continuous Manufacturing: Why Biosimilar Producers Struggle
description: In the latest episode of the Bioprocessing Unfiltered podcast, Anurag Rathore of the Indian Institute of Technology, Delhi, breaks down one of the key barriers holding back the widespread adoption of continuous manufacturing in biopharmaceuticals. Rathore explains that retrofitting an existing batch manufacturing facility for continuous processing is rarely practical — the extent of the changes required makes it financially unviable, and the disruption to ongoing commercial production compounds the challenge. This means companies effectively need to build new facilities from the ground up. For biosimilar producers, who typically operate with tighter budgets than innovator companies, that level of capital investment is a significant hurdle despite the long-term profitability continuous manufacturing can offer. As a result, Rathore notes, it is largely the innovator companies that are leading the way in implementing continuous manufacturing today.

title: Levers For Streamlining And Optimizing The Biosimilar Process
description:
New and more advanced production methods mean biosimilar developers can produce their own versions of commercial drugs with greater efficiency. Levers like cell line engineering and bioreactor controls make it easier to increase productivity. Biologics Consulting Group Principal Consultant Vince Narbut walked through some of the unit operations ripe for optimizing during Bioprocess Online Live: Process Control's Increasing Role In Biosimilar Approval.

When changing key processes, it is important to aim for the mid-range of reference product attribute data to ensure consistent similarity, since developers are now less likely to have clinical efficacy study data to fall back on.

title: In Biosimilar Analytical Development, Is A CQA Ever Not Critical?
description:
The word "critical" implies a binary signal. The attribute is either existentially important or it's not.

In biosimilar development, there is a hierarchy of critical quality attributes (CQAs) to monitor during the comparative analytical assessment (CAA). During Bioprocess Online Live: Process Control's Increasing Role In Biosimilar Approval, Biologics Consulting Group Principal Consultant Diana Colleluori said that attributes relating to immunogenicity and function pose a higher risk and must be closely monitored.

title: Building A Comprehensive Control Strategy For Biosimilar Analytics
description:
Like many other biologic drugs, building a comprehensive controls strategy for biosimilars starts with defining critical quality attributes (CQAs), said Vince Narbut, a principal consultant at Biologics Consulting Group, during Bioprocess Online Live: Process Control's Increasing Role In Biosimilar Approval.

From there, biosimilar sponsors must map out the critical process parameters (CPPs) used to control upstream and downstream manufacturing, he said. It starts to get tricky when you introduce the originator product's specification range. Narbut said most of the iterative adjustments happen on the upstream side where you can tweak glycan profiles and charge variants.

title: How To Avoid A Biosimilar Comparative Efficacy Study, If Possible
description:
Few companies, if any, would ever eagerly volunteer to perform a comparative efficacy study (CES) for their biosimilar candidate. The FDA has been clear all along that compelling a CES remains a tool in its toolbox if the agency believes it's necessary. So what might trigger one, and how can companies avoid it?

During Bioprocess Online Live: Process Control's Increasing Role In Biosimilar Approval, Cecilia Michel, managing director and head of research and development strategy at Alvotech, said the comparative analytical assessment (CAA) is key. The analytical package should include at a minimum orthogonal assays, both physical/chemical, potency, and binding, among others, to truly understand your molecule and its mechanism of action.

Early and ongoing engagement with the FDA is also important.

title: In The U.S., Pharmacy-Level Biosimilar Substitution Remains A High Bar
description:
Recent changes in the FDA's biosimilarity assessment guidance do not address the other side of the biosimilar coin, interchangeability. Unique to the U.S., pharmacy-level substitution is allowed only when companies clear an additional regulatory hurdle of receiving an interchangeability designation.

During Bioprocess Online Live: Process Control's Increasing Role In Biosimilar Approval, Diana Colleluori, a principal consultant at Biologics Consulting Group, said that, from her perspective, interchangeability remains a formidable obstacle. However, when it comes to the decline of switching studies, once necessary for interchangeability, FDA now puts greater emphasis on multiple functional assays.

title: The Burden Of Proof Has Shifted To Analytics For Biosimilar Approval
description:
The FDA's recent and stunning declaration that comparative analytical assessments (CAA) are generally more sensitive than clinical efficacy studies (CES) shows the great degree in which the agency is leaning on analytics rather than clinical data when considering 351(k) applications for biosimilars.

During Bioprocess Online Live: Process Control's Increasing Role In Biosimilar Approval, Diana Colleluori, a principal consultant at Biologics Consulting Group, explained that it shows FDA is learning along with the rest of us that CES is not the definitive biosimilarity indicator we thought it was.

title: What Is a Biosimilar? Is It the Same as a Biologic? | A Rheumatologist Explains
description:
Your doctor just mentioned a "biosimilar" and you nodded along — but had no idea what they meant.

You're not alone. And you deserve a real explanation.

Here's what every Rheumatoid Arthritis, Psoriatic Arthritis, and Ankylosing Spondylitis patient needs to know:

🧬 WHAT IS A BIOLOGIC?

Biologics are complex medicines made from living cells — designed to target the exact immune pathways driving your inflammation. Think Humira (adalimumab), Enbrel (etanercept), Remicade (infliximab), Cosentyx, Taltz. They transformed autoimmune disease care. They are also expensive — sometimes $100,000+ per year.

💊 WHAT IS A BIOSIMILAR?

A biosimilar is NOT a generic drug. It is a highly similar — but not identical — copy of a reference biologic, approved by the FDA only after rigorous testing to confirm:

✅ Same mechanism of action
✅ Same safety profile
✅ Same clinical efficacy
✅ Same dosage and delivery method

Think of it like this: a generic drug is an exact chemical copy. A biosimilar is the closest possible copy of an incredibly complex biological molecule — proven equivalent through years of clinical trials.

💰 WHY DOES THIS MATTER FOR YOU?
Biosimilars can cost less than the original biologic.
That means:
→ Insurance coverage that was denied may now be approved
→ More patients can access life-changing treatment

For RA, Psoriatic Arthritis, and Ankylosing Spondylitis — the most common biosimilars you may encounter include:
🔹 Adalimumab biosimilars (Humira alternatives): Amjevita, Hadlima, Hyrimoz, 🔹 Infliximab biosimilars (Remicade alternatives): Inflectra, Renflexis

description:

We use the "Lemonade vs. Soufflé" analogy to explain why biologics are fundamentally different from traditional generic drugs and explore the rigorous FDA pathway required to prove they are "highly similar" to the brand-name original.

𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗧𝗮𝗸𝗲𝗮𝘄𝗮𝘆𝘀:

• 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗕𝗶𝗼𝗹𝗼𝗴𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲𝘅𝗶𝘁𝘆: Understand why traditional drugs are like simple lemonade (easy to copy exactly), while biologics are like a master chef’s soufflé—grown inside living cells and hundreds of times larger and more complex.
• 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗕𝗣𝗖𝗜 𝗔𝗰𝘁 (𝟮𝟬𝟬𝟵): Learn about the landmark legislation that created the 351(k) abbreviated licensure pathway, allowing for the approval of biosimilar and interchangeable products.
• 𝗣𝗵𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝟭: 𝗔𝗻𝗮𝗹𝘆𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗼𝗻: Discover the "microscopic inspection" phase, where the FDA ensures the biosimilar’s 3D molecular shape and active structures line up perfectly with the reference product to meet the "highly similar" standard.
• 𝗣𝗵𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝟮: 𝗖𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗼𝗻: Beyond the lab, we explore the real-world human trials required to prove there are no clinically meaningful differences in safety, purity, or potency.
• 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆 & 𝗦𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗦𝘁𝘂𝗱𝗶𝗲𝘀: A look at the "gold standard" designation that requires extra evidence to prove patients can alternate between the original and the biosimilar without any loss of efficacy or safety risks.
• 𝗣𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗺𝗮𝗰𝗶𝘀𝘁 𝗦𝘂𝗯𝘀𝘁𝗶𝘁𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻: Understanding how state laws dictate whether a pharmacist can automatically swap a brand-name biologic for an interchangeable biosimilar at the counter without a new prescription.

title: ANALYTICAL RELEASE TESTING of Biosimilars: A Practical Overview
description:
Analytical Methods and Importance

Before a biosimilar drug product can be released for patient use, it must undergo extensive analytical testing to ensure safety, quality, purity, and potency. Because biosimilars are complex protein-based medicines, multiple analytical methods are required to confirm consistency and biological activity.

This video provides an overview of biosimilar drug product release testing and explains the importance of each analytical method used in quality control laboratories.

The following tests are covered in this video:
• Appearance (color and clarity)
• pH measurement
• Osmolality testing
• Size Exclusion Chromatography (SEC)
• Ion Exchange Chromatography (IEX)
• Reverse Phase HPLC (RP-HPLC)
• Endotoxin testing (BET)
• Visible and subvisible particulate testing
• Potency assays
• Cell-based assays
• Sterility testing

Each test is explained with its scientific principle and importance in ensuring biosimilar product quality and patient safety.

title: CH322 Biologics and Biosimilars as Therapeutic Agents
description:
In this lecture from CH322 Medicinal Chemistry & Pharmacology, we explore the expanding role of biologics in modern drug development.

Unlike traditional small molecules, biologics are large, complex therapeutic agents derived from living systems. Their activity depends on higher-order structure, recombinant expression, and highly specific molecular recognition.

Topics covered in this lecture include:

• What defines a biologic drug
• Small molecules vs biologics — key pharmacological differences
• Antibody structure and mechanism of action
• Blocking ligand–receptor signaling pathways
• Case study: Nemolizumab (Nemluvio) and IL-31 in atopic dermatitis
• Pharmacokinetics of monoclonal antibodies (absorption, distribution, elimination)
• Monoclonal vs polyclonal antibodies
• Rabies immune globulin and post-exposure prophylaxis
• Limitations of antibody therapeutics
• Immunogenicity and anti-drug antibodies
• Manufacturing challenges and cost
• Biological escape mechanisms
• Biosimilars vs generics — regulatory and structural considerations

This lecture highlights why medicinal chemistry must now include biologics as a central pillar of modern pharmacotherapy.

Designed for upper-division undergraduate and graduate students in chemistry, biochemistry, and pharmacology.

In this video, we break down Nufymco (ranibizumab-leyk) vs Lucentis and explain what FDA interchangeable biosimilar status really means for patients living with serious retinal diseases.You’ll learn how Nufymco works to protect vision in wet age-related macular degeneration (wet AMD), diabetic macular edema (DME), diabetic retinopathy, retinal vein occlusion, and myopic choroidal neovascularization (myopic CNV). We explain in simple terms how VEGF causes abnormal blood vessel growth in the eye, and how anti-VEGF treatments like Nufymco help block this process to reduce swelling, slow vision loss, and in many cases improve sight.This patient-focused explainer also covers:• What makes Nufymco interchangeable with Lucentis
• How intravitreal injections are given and what to expect during treatment
• Potential benefits and common side effects
• Why biosimilars matter for affordability and access to retinal care

title: The Ovarian Cancer Drug Wall Street Is Ignoring | Dr. Stella Vnook, Kaeda Biopharma
description:
Ovarian cancer kills more women than any other gynecologic cancer — and most patients are diagnosed too late, on toxic generic platinum therapies, with recurrence within 12–18 months. Dr. Stella Vnook, co-founder and CEO of Kaeda Biopharma, is on a mission to change that.

In this episode of Invst Guru, Jeff "Fuzzy" Wenzel sits down with Dr. Vnook to talk about KAD101 — a first-in-class biologic designed to block the prolactin receptor, which is overexpressed in roughly 80% of ovarian cancer patients. Named after Kaeda, the dragon that eats its own tail, the drug triggers a process called autophagy, essentially causing cancer cells to self-destruct. Early Phase 1 data showed tumor reductions in all three patients dosed, with a strikingly tolerable side-effect profile.

But this conversation goes way beyond the science. Dr. Vnook — who lost her own mother to ovarian cancer — pulls back the curtain on what it's really like to raise capital for women's health biotech in 2026: the 40% NIH funding cut, the IPO collapse from 100+ biotechs in 2021 down to a handful, Trump's Most Favored Nation executive order, HR 7837, and why so many investors are quietly redirecting capital from pharma into AI and fintech.

If you're an accredited investor curious about biotech, a founder navigating the FDA, or someone whose family has been touched by ovarian cancer — this one matters.

title: What Chemo Does to Cancer Nurses
description: What Chemo Does to Cancer Nurses. Sources- PMID 32920100 c4news on TT Chemotherapy drugs are designed to be highly toxic to rapidly dividing cells, making them incredibly effective against tumors but inherently hazardous to healthy human tissue. Oncology nurses handle these potent antineoplastic agents daily, and without rigorous safety protocols, they risk exposure through inhaled microscopic aerosols, accidental skin contact, or the handling of contaminated bodily fluids. Because these aggressive chemicals cannot distinguish between cancerous and healthy cells, continuous, low-level occupational exposure can quietly accumulate in a nurse's system over time, silently disrupting normal cellular division and causing hidden chromosomal damage. Over years of dedicated service, this cumulative exposure can lead to severe long-term health consequences, including reproductive toxicity, an increased risk of miscarriages, and paradoxically, the development of secondary occupational cancers such as leukemia. To prevent healthcare professionals from suffering the very diseases they are working to treat, strict adherence to comprehensive safety standards, including the use of impermeable gowns and closed-system drug transfer devices, is absolutely essential. These protective measures act as a vital, non-negotiable barrier, ensuring that the life-saving treatments nurses administer to their patients do not ultimately compromise their own health and futures. #health #chemotherapy #cancer

title: How Gleevec Revolutionized Cancer Treatment
description:
In 1995, Mel Mann faced a grim cancer diagnosis with just three years to live. Diagnosed with chronic myeloid leukemia, he volunteered for clinical trials, but nothing worked until he tried Gleevec in 1998. This targeted therapy transformed his life, allowing him to run a marathon just months later. Gleevec was one of the first drugs to target the genetic cause of cancer, specifically the Philadelphia chromosome. Developed by oncologist Brian Druker, Gleevec offered a new approach to cancer treatment, focusing on stopping cancer at its source rather than just attacking cells. This innovation marked a significant shift in oncology, paving the way for future targeted therapies. As we reflect on Gleevec's legacy, the ongoing advancements in cancer treatment continue to inspire hope for patients worldwide.
